title: Crisis Communication
subtitle: Announce bad news, face the backlash, and rebuild what a crisis costs you

lessons.title: Annoncer une mauvaise nouvelle
lessons.description: Deliver difficult news clearly, honestly, and with genuine empathy — before the story gets told without you.

blocks.heading: Dire vite, dire vrai
blocks.body: The first rule of crisis communication is timing: an organisation that announces bad news itself controls the narrative; one that waits for it to leak is instantly on the defensive. The second rule is honesty: a measured, uncomfortable truth costs far less, over time, than a comforting half-truth that later unravels in public.

examples.french: Nous avons choisi de vous informer avant que la presse ne s'en charge.
examples.english: We chose to inform you before the press took charge of it.

examples.french: Mieux vaut une vérité inconfortable qu'un silence qui se retourne contre nous.
examples.english: An uncomfortable truth is better than a silence that backfires on us.

examples.french: La transparence désamorce davantage de critiques qu'une stratégie de communication habile.
examples.english: Transparency defuses more criticism than a clever communication strategy.

examples.french: Nous préférons annoncer nous-mêmes une mauvaise nouvelle plutôt que la voir fuiter.
examples.english: We prefer to announce bad news ourselves rather than see it leak out.

blocks.tip: If a fact is likely to reach the press within 48 hours, announce it yourself within 24 — the gap between the two timelines is where reputations are lost.

blocks.heading: Nommer les faits sans les euphémiser
blocks.body: Crisis French resists two temptations at once: sensationalism and euphemism. A serious problem should be named with plain, specific vocabulary — not dramatised, but not hidden behind vague corporate phrasing either. Saying "un léger contretemps" about a data breach affecting thousands of people is a credibility risk in itself.

examples.french: Nous avons identifié une défaillance dans notre système de sécurité.
examples.english: We have identified a failure in our security system.

examples.french: Cet incident a affecté environ dix mille utilisateurs.
examples.english: This incident affected approximately ten thousand users.

examples.french: Nous reconnaissons la gravité de la situation.
examples.english: We acknowledge the seriousness of the situation.

examples.french: Il ne s'agit pas d'un simple contretemps, mais d'un dysfonctionnement sérieux.
examples.english: This is not a minor hitch, but a serious malfunction.

blocks.tip: Watch for euphemism creep: "contretemps", "anomalie", "souci technique" are all words crisis communicators reach for to soften a serious fact — a careful listener learns to hear through them.

blocks.heading: S'excuser sincèrement, sans se dédouaner
blocks.body: A real apology names what went wrong, takes ownership of it, and stops there — it does not immediately pivot to context, excuses, or blame. The word "mais" is the most dangerous word in an apology: everything after it tends to erase everything before it, in the listener's mind.

examples.french: Nous vous présentons nos excuses les plus sincères.
examples.english: We offer you our most sincere apologies.

examples.french: Nous assumons pleinement la responsabilité de cette erreur.
examples.english: We fully take responsibility for this mistake.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas un incident isolé imputable à un seul employé, c'est une défaillance collective.
examples.english: This is not an isolated incident attributable to one employee, it is a collective failure.

examples.french: Nos excuses ne suffisent pas ; nous devons aussi agir.
examples.english: Our apologies are not enough; we must also act.

blocks.tip: Test your own apology: if you can insert "mais" after it without changing the meaning, it probably was not a full apology in the first place.

blocks.heading: Le passif pour nommer un fait sans désigner un coupable
blocks.body: The passive voice lets a spokesperson state what happened without either hiding it or turning it into a public trial of one employee. "Une erreur a été commise" names the fact; it does not yet assign blame, which is often appropriate in the first hours of a crisis, before an investigation is complete. Used honestly — followed later by real accountability — this is not evasion; used forever, it becomes exactly that.

examples.french: Une erreur a été commise dans le traitement de ces données.
examples.english: A mistake was made in the handling of this data.

examples.french: Des mesures ont été prises dès la découverte de l'incident.
examples.english: Measures were taken as soon as the incident was discovered.

examples.french: Les personnes concernées ont été informées sans délai.
examples.english: The people affected were informed without delay.

examples.french: Une enquête interne a été ouverte pour établir les responsabilités exactes.
examples.english: An internal inquiry has been opened to establish exactly where responsibility lies.

blocks.tip: The passive buys you time to investigate before naming names — but a crisis statement that stays passive forever, even after the facts are known, starts to sound like an admission that no one wants to be found.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel journalistique et le futur de l'engagement
blocks.body: When a figure is not yet confirmed, careful French uses the conditional to report it responsibly: "le nombre de personnes touchées serait d'environ dix mille" signals a working estimate, not a verified fact. Once a commitment is firm, the simple future replaces it: "nous publierons", "nous mettrons en place" — no hedge, no conditional, because a promise about the future should not sound tentative.

examples.french: Le nombre de personnes touchées serait d'environ dix mille, selon les premières estimations.
examples.english: The number of people affected is thought to be around ten thousand, according to initial estimates.

examples.french: L'origine de la défaillance ne serait pas encore totalement établie.
examples.english: The cause of the failure is not thought to be fully established yet.

examples.french: Nous mettrons en place un dispositif de suivi dès demain.
examples.english: We will set up a follow-up system starting tomorrow.

examples.french: Un rapport complet sera publié d'ici la fin du mois.
examples.english: A full report will be published by the end of the month.

blocks.tip: Never use the conditional for your own commitments — "nous ferions le nécessaire" sounds like a promise you might break; "nous ferons le nécessaire" sounds like one you intend to keep.

passages.title: L'annonce chez NordTech
passages.french:
Un vendredi soir, Solenne Vasseur, directrice de la communication de NordTech, reçut un appel qu'elle redoutait depuis des mois : une défaillance dans le système de sécurité avait exposé les données de milliers d'utilisateurs.
Elle convoqua aussitôt une cellule de crise et rejoignit Marc Delannoy, le PDG, dans son bureau.
« Le nombre de personnes touchées serait d'environ dix mille, selon les premières estimations, expliqua-t-elle. L'origine de la défaillance ne serait pas encore totalement établie. »
« Attendons d'en savoir plus avant de communiquer », proposa Marc, visiblement tenté par le silence.
« C'est précisément ce qu'il ne faut pas faire, répondit Solenne sans détour. Nous préférons annoncer nous-mêmes une mauvaise nouvelle plutôt que la voir fuiter. »
Elle rédigea un communiqué en une heure, le relut deux fois, puis le tendit à Marc.
« Une erreur a été commise dans le traitement de ces données, lut-il à voix haute. Nous en assumons pleinement la responsabilité. »
« Il ne s'agit pas d'un simple contretemps, ajouta Solenne, mais d'un dysfonctionnement sérieux. Le dire autrement serait mentir. »
Marc hésita sur la dernière phrase. « Et les excuses ? »
« Sincères, et sans "mais", précisa-t-elle. Sinon, personne n'y croira. »
Le communiqué fut diffusé avant minuit, accompagné d'une conférence de presse fixée au lendemain matin.
À vingt-trois heures cinquante-cinq, Solenne relut une dernière fois la phrase finale : « Nous mettrons en place un dispositif de suivi dès demain. » Pas de conditionnel. Un engagement.
passages.english:
One Friday evening, Solenne Vasseur, head of communications at NordTech, received a call she had dreaded for months: a failure in the security system had exposed the data of thousands of users.
She immediately convened a crisis unit and joined Marc Delannoy, the CEO, in his office.
"The number of people affected is thought to be around ten thousand, according to initial estimates," she explained. "The cause of the failure is not thought to be fully established yet."
"Let's wait to know more before communicating," suggested Marc, visibly tempted by silence.
"That is precisely what we must not do," Solenne replied without hesitation. "We prefer to announce bad news ourselves rather than see it leak out."
She drafted a statement within the hour, reread it twice, then handed it to Marc.
"A mistake was made in the handling of this data," he read aloud. "We fully take responsibility for it."
"This is not a minor hitch," Solenne added, "but a serious malfunction. Saying otherwise would be lying."
Marc hesitated over the last line. "And the apology?"
"Sincere, and without a 'but'," she specified. "Otherwise, no one will believe it."
The statement was released before midnight, along with a press conference set for the next morning.
At eleven fifty-five, Solenne reread the final line one last time: "We will set up a follow-up system starting tomorrow." No conditional. A commitment.

lessons.title: Répondre à une polémique
lessons.description: Face public criticism without losing composure, correct the record, and know when silence would cost more than a response.

blocks.heading: Distinguer le fait de l'interprétation
blocks.body: When a controversy erupts, the fastest way to lose control of it is to respond to every interpretation as if it were a fact. A disciplined spokesperson separates the two explicitly: confirm or correct the facts first, and only then, if at all, address the interpretation built on top of them. Conflating the two invites an argument that can never be settled with evidence.

examples.french: Nous contestons l'interprétation, pas les faits eux-mêmes.
examples.english: We are disputing the interpretation, not the facts themselves.

examples.french: Il convient de distinguer ce qui relève du fait de ce qui relève de l'opinion.
examples.english: It is worth distinguishing what belongs to fact from what belongs to opinion.

examples.french: Cette polémique repose sur une confusion entre une hypothèse et une certitude.
examples.english: This controversy rests on a confusion between a hypothesis and a certainty.

examples.french: Rectifions d'abord les faits ; nous reviendrons ensuite sur le fond.
examples.english: Let's correct the facts first; we will come back to the substance afterward.

blocks.tip: "Le fait que" introduces something the speaker treats as an established truth; watch which mode follows it — it often reveals whether the speaker actually believes the fact or is merely conceding it for argument's sake.

blocks.heading: Répondre sans attiser
blocks.body: Not every accusation deserves a reply, and not every reply should match the temperature of the attack that provoked it. A measured response, even to a loud controversy, tends to shorten it; an emotional counter-attack almost always extends it. Knowing when silence is a strategy — not a failure to respond — is itself a C1-level judgment call.

examples.french: Nous ne répondrons pas à chaque accusation, mais nous répondrons sur le fond.
examples.english: We will not respond to every accusation, but we will respond on the substance.

examples.french: Le silence, ici, aurait été interprété comme un aveu.
examples.english: Silence, here, would have been read as an admission.

examples.french: Riposter à chaud aggrave presque toujours la polémique.
examples.english: Striking back in the heat of the moment almost always makes the controversy worse.

examples.french: Mieux vaut une réponse posée qu'une réplique impulsive.
examples.english: A composed response is better than an impulsive retort.

blocks.tip: Before answering an angry message publicly, ask whether silence would read as guilt or simply as restraint — the two require completely different responses.

blocks.heading: Corriger sans humilier — la mise au point
blocks.body: A "mise au point" corrects the record without turning the correction into a personal attack on whoever spread the error. It states what is inaccurate, cites what is actually true, and stops — it does not need to mock the source of the mistake to be effective, and mockery usually reopens the controversy rather than closing it.

examples.french: Nous tenons à apporter une mise au point sur plusieurs points inexacts.
examples.english: We would like to set the record straight on several inaccurate points.

examples.french: Cette rumeur, largement relayée, ne repose sur aucune source vérifiée.
examples.english: This rumour, widely shared, is not based on any verified source.

examples.french: Nous démentons formellement toute implication de notre part.
examples.english: We formally deny any involvement on our part.

examples.french: Corriger une erreur n'est pas humilier celui qui l'a commise.
examples.english: Correcting a mistake is not humiliating the person who made it.

blocks.tip: A "mise au point" that names and shames the original source usually gets shared more than the correction itself — keep the focus on the facts, not on who got them wrong.

blocks.heading: Le fait que + indicatif ou subjonctif — cadrer un fait contesté
blocks.body: "Le fait que" can take either mode, and the choice is meaningful: the indicative treats what follows as an established truth, while the subjunctive frames it as something merely alleged, circulating, or not yet proven. In a controversy, switching from indicative to subjunctive mid-statement is a precise way of downgrading a claim without ever calling the other side a liar outright.

examples.french: Le fait que cette rumeur circule ne signifie pas qu'elle soit fondée.
examples.english: The fact that this rumour is circulating does not mean it is well-founded.

examples.french: Le fait que nous ayons réagi vite montre notre sérieux.
examples.english: The fact that we reacted quickly shows our seriousness.

examples.french: Le fait qu'un chiffre soit repris partout ne le rend pas exact pour autant.
examples.english: The fact that a figure is repeated everywhere does not make it accurate.

examples.french: Le fait que la source reste anonyme invite à la prudence.
examples.english: The fact that the source remains anonymous calls for caution.

blocks.tip: Indicative after "le fait que" quietly concedes the point as true; subjunctive keeps it at arm's length — choose deliberately, since your audience will register the difference even if they cannot name it.

blocks.heading: Ce n'est pas X, c'est Y — la restriction pour recadrer un débat
blocks.body: The cleft construction "ce n'est pas X, c'est Y" is the C1 speaker's sharpest tool for correcting a controversy's framing in one breath: it names the wrong emphasis and replaces it with the right one, in a single balanced sentence. Paired with the restrictive "ne... que", it also lets a spokesperson narrow exactly what is, and is not, being disputed.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas une erreur, c'est une décision assumée.
examples.english: It is not a mistake, it is a decision we stand by.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas le montant qui pose problème, c'est la manière dont il a été annoncé.
examples.english: It is not the amount that is the problem, it is the way it was announced.

examples.french: Nous ne contestons que l'interprétation, pas les chiffres eux-mêmes.
examples.english: We are disputing only the interpretation, not the figures themselves.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas nous qui avons lancé cette rumeur, c'est un compte anonyme.
examples.english: We are not the ones who started this rumour, it was an anonymous account.

blocks.tip: "Ce n'est pas X, c'est Y" works best when X is what the public already believes and Y is the correction — leading with the misconception, briefly, makes the correction land harder.

passages.title: La polémique enfle
passages.french:
Dix jours après l'annonce, une capture d'écran tronquée du communiqué de NordTech devint virale, laissant croire que l'entreprise avait attendu une semaine avant d'agir.
Solenne fut contactée par Inès Kader, journaliste spécialisée dans le numérique, pour une interview en direct.
« On vous accuse d'avoir dissimulé l'incident pendant plusieurs jours, attaqua Inès d'entrée. Que répondez-vous ? »
« Nous contestons l'interprétation, pas les faits eux-mêmes, répondit Solenne sans se démonter. Le communiqué original porte une date et une heure, vérifiables par n'importe qui. »
« Cette rumeur circule pourtant largement, insista la journaliste. — Le fait qu'elle circule ne signifie pas qu'elle soit fondée, précisa Solenne. Nous démentons formellement tout délai de plusieurs jours. »
Inès tenta une question piège : « N'auriez-vous pas simplement cherché un bouc émissaire en interne ? »
« Ce n'est pas une erreur individuelle que nous avons cherché à punir, répliqua Solenne, gardant son sang-froid, c'est une défaillance collective que nous avons choisi d'assumer, publiquement, dès le premier soir. »
Elle ne haussa pas la voix, ne coupa pas la parole, et ne laissa passer aucune inexactitude sans la rectifier.
À la fin de l'entretien, NordTech publia une mise au point détaillée, accompagnée de l'horodatage complet du communiqué original.
La pression médiatique retomba en deux jours. La polémique, elle, ne s'éteignit pas immédiatement — mais elle cessa, au moins, de porter sur des faits inexacts.
passages.english:
Ten days after the announcement, a truncated screenshot of NordTech's statement went viral, suggesting the company had waited a week before acting.
Solenne was contacted by Inès Kader, a journalist specialising in digital affairs, for a live interview.
"You are accused of having concealed the incident for several days," Inès opened aggressively. "What is your response?"
"We are disputing the interpretation, not the facts themselves," Solenne replied, unshaken. "The original statement carries a date and a time, verifiable by anyone."
"This rumour is nonetheless circulating widely," the journalist insisted. "The fact that it is circulating does not mean it is well-founded," Solenne specified. "We formally deny any delay of several days."
Inès tried a loaded question: "Didn't you simply look for a scapegoat internally?"
"It is not an individual mistake that we sought to punish," Solenne replied, keeping her cool, "it is a collective failure that we chose to own, publicly, on the very first evening."
She did not raise her voice, did not interrupt, and let no inaccuracy pass without correcting it.
At the end of the interview, NordTech published a detailed clarification, together with the full timestamp of the original statement.
Media pressure eased within two days. The controversy itself did not die out immediately — but it stopped, at least, being about inaccurate facts.

lessons.title: Reconstruire la confiance
lessons.description: Turn an apology into action: concrete measures, real follow-through, and the patience trust repair actually requires.

blocks.heading: Des actes, pas seulement des mots
blocks.body: An apology opens the door to trust repair; it does not walk through it. What actually rebuilds confidence is a series of concrete, verifiable actions that match the scale of the harm — a corrective measure with a date attached is worth far more, in this register, than a heartfelt but vague promise to "do better".

examples.french: Des excuses ne suffisent pas ; il faut des actes qui les prouvent.
examples.english: Apologies are not enough; they need actions to prove them.

examples.french: Nous avons mis en place des mesures correctives concrètes, avec un calendrier précis.
examples.english: We have put in place concrete corrective measures, with a precise timeline.

examples.french: La confiance ne se restaure pas par une phrase, mais par une série de preuves.
examples.english: Trust is not restored by a single sentence, but by a series of proofs.

examples.french: Chaque engagement pris doit être suivi d'un compte rendu public.
examples.english: Every commitment made must be followed by a public account of progress.

blocks.tip: If a corrective measure cannot be given a date, it is still an intention, not yet a commitment — say so plainly rather than dressing it up as more than it is.

blocks.heading: La reddition de comptes — rendre compte dans la durée
blocks.body: Accountability, in this register, is not a single confession but a habit: regular, dated updates that let outsiders check progress against what was promised. An independent audit carries more weight than an internal reassurance, precisely because it removes the organisation's own interest from the judgment.

examples.french: Nous nous engageons à publier un rapport de suivi tous les trimestres.
examples.english: We commit to publishing a follow-up report every quarter.

examples.french: Un audit indépendant a été commandé pour garantir l'objectivité du diagnostic.
examples.english: An independent audit was commissioned to guarantee the objectivity of the diagnosis.

examples.french: Rendre compte régulièrement vaut mieux qu'une promesse unique, vite oubliée.
examples.english: Reporting back regularly is worth more than a single promise, soon forgotten.

examples.french: La reddition de comptes n'est pas un aveu de faiblesse, c'est un gage de sérieux.
examples.english: Accountability is not an admission of weakness, it is a sign of seriousness.

blocks.tip: "Rendre compte" (to report back, to be accountable) is not the same construction as "se rendre compte" (to realise) — the reflexive pronoun changes the meaning entirely.

blocks.heading: Le temps long — la patience et la constance
blocks.body: Trust rebuilds on a different clock than a crisis breaks it: slowly, and only through consistency sustained well past the point where the story has left the headlines. Declaring victory too early is one of the most common and most damaging errors in this final phase — it invites exactly the scrutiny that a still-fragile reputation cannot yet survive.

examples.french: La confiance se regagne lentement, geste après geste.
examples.english: Trust is won back slowly, one gesture at a time.

examples.french: Rien ne serait pire que de crier victoire trop tôt.
examples.english: Nothing would be worse than declaring victory too soon.

examples.french: Notre crédibilité se reconstruira sur la durée, pas sur un seul communiqué.
examples.english: Our credibility will rebuild over time, not through a single statement.

examples.french: La constance, plus que l'éclat, restaure une réputation.
examples.english: Consistency, more than any grand gesture, restores a reputation.

blocks.tip: The moment a team feels ready to stop talking about a crisis is often the exact moment it should keep one more update on the calendar — relief is not the same as proof.

blocks.heading: Le futur antérieur — projeter la confiance retrouvée
blocks.body: The futur antérieur describes an action that will be complete before another future point — exactly the shape of a trust-repair timeline, where each milestone only matters once it is finished. "Quand l'audit aura été rendu public" places the audience in a future where judgment is finally possible, because the evidence, by then, already exists.

examples.french: Nous aurons publié trois rapports de suivi avant la fin de l'année.
examples.english: We will have published three follow-up reports before the end of the year.

examples.french: Quand l'audit aura été rendu public, chacun pourra juger sur pièces.
examples.english: Once the audit has been made public, everyone will be able to judge for themselves.

examples.french: La confiance ne sera restaurée que lorsque les faits auront été vérifiés.
examples.english: Trust will only be restored once the facts have been verified.

examples.french: Une fois les mesures correctives mises en œuvre, nous referons un point complet.
examples.english: Once the corrective measures have been implemented, we will do a full review.

blocks.tip: The futur antérieur lets you promise a future without pretending it has already arrived — it names the finish line precisely, instead of vaguely gesturing toward "soon".

blocks.heading: Plus... plus... et à condition que — la confiance est proportionnelle à l'effort
blocks.body: The correlative structure "plus... plus..." (the more... the more...) lets a C1 speaker state, almost mathematically, that trust scales with visible effort — it is a way of setting expectations honestly rather than promising an instant fix. "À condition que" (+ subjunctive) makes that same proportionality explicit as a condition, not a hope.

examples.french: Plus les preuves seront nombreuses, plus la confiance reviendra vite.
examples.english: The more evidence there is, the faster trust will return.

examples.french: La réputation ne se redressera qu'à condition que les engagements soient tenus.
examples.english: The reputation will only recover provided the commitments are kept.

examples.french: Moins nous communiquerons sur ce sujet, plus les doutes persisteront.
examples.english: The less we communicate on this subject, the longer doubts will persist.

examples.french: À condition de rester constants, nous regagnerons ce que nous avons perdu.
examples.english: Provided we remain consistent, we will win back what we lost.

blocks.tip: "À condition que" takes the subjunctive; its cousin "à condition de" takes the infinitive when the subject of both clauses is the same — do not mix the two constructions.

passages.title: Un an après
passages.french:
Un an, presque jour pour jour, après la défaillance qui avait exposé les données de milliers d'utilisateurs, Solenne présenta le quatrième rapport de suivi de NordTech devant un parterre de journalistes, dont Inès Kader, redevenue simple observatrice.
« Nous aurons publié quatre rapports de suivi d'ici la fin de la semaine, commença Solenne. Chacun a été relu par un cabinet indépendant avant diffusion. »
Elle présenta les mesures correctives une à une : un nouveau protocole de sécurité, une cellule de veille permanente, une procédure d'alerte réduite à moins d'une heure.
« L'audit indépendant a validé chacune de ces mesures, précisa-t-elle. Ce n'est pas nous qui l'affirmons ; ce sont les données qui le montrent. »
Un journaliste l'interrompit : « Considérez-vous la crise comme terminée ? »
« Rien ne serait pire que de crier victoire trop tôt, répondit Solenne sans hésiter. Notre crédibilité se reconstruira sur la durée, pas sur un seul rapport, aussi complet soit-il. »
Inès, silencieuse depuis le début, leva enfin la main. « Qu'avez-vous appris de cette année ? »
« Que la patience compte autant que la méthode, répondit Solenne après un instant. Et que la constance, plus que l'éclat, restaure une réputation. »
À la sortie, un utilisateur interrogé par une chaîne locale résuma, sans le savoir, l'essentiel : « Je ne leur fais pas encore entièrement confiance. Mais je reconnais qu'ils ont tenu parole, mois après mois. »
Ce n'était pas encore une victoire. C'était, exactement, ce que Solenne avait visé depuis le premier soir.
passages.english:
One year, almost to the day, after the failure that had exposed the data of thousands of users, Solenne presented NordTech's fourth follow-up report before a room full of journalists, including Inès Kader, now merely an observer.
"We will have published four follow-up reports by the end of the week," Solenne began. "Each one was reviewed by an independent firm before release."
She presented the corrective measures one by one: a new security protocol, a permanent monitoring unit, an alert procedure reduced to under an hour.
"The independent audit validated each of these measures," she specified. "It is not us saying so; it is the data that shows it."
A journalist interrupted her. "Do you consider the crisis over?"
"Nothing would be worse than declaring victory too soon," Solenne replied without hesitation. "Our credibility will rebuild over time, not through a single report, however thorough it may be."
Inès, silent until then, finally raised her hand. "What have you learned from this year?"
"That patience matters as much as method," Solenne answered after a moment. "And that consistency, more than any grand gesture, restores a reputation."
On the way out, a user interviewed by a local channel unknowingly summed up the essential point: "I don't fully trust them yet. But I recognise they have kept their word, month after month."
It was not yet a victory. It was, exactly, what Solenne had aimed for since the very first evening.
